info.title: Bi-Factor Generalized Cognitive Diagnosis Model Framework

author.affiliation:
Autonomous University of Madrid
								
									Madrid
									Spain

text.text: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) are often applied to constructs that are largely unidimensional in nature (e.g., mathematics, reading, mental health status) where a set of discrete attributes coexists with a dominant general proficiency dimension.

This article presents the bi-factor CDM model (BF-CDM), which partitions item responses into a direct effect of continuous general proficiency and a discrete attribute-mastery tier, allowing mastery classifications to be made beyond what is attributable to general ability.
By modeling both tiers explicitly, the BF-CDM makes it possible to evaluate the contribution of the discrete tier itself.

Specifically, it can show whether the hypothesized attributes carry diagnostic information beyond general proficiency, both through model comparison with the nested unidimensional model and through the reliability of the attribute-specific component.

A simulation study manipulating sample size, test length, number of attributes, and attribute-tier discrimination shows accurate recovery of item and person parameters, and of the modelimplied response functions.

An application to reading comprehension data from PISA illustrates the practical value of the model: reliability of attribute-mastery classifications drops substantially once variance attributable to general proficiency is partialled out, indicating that much of the apparent diagnostic precision obtained under a saturated attribute structure reflects a single dominant general factor.
In educational and psychological measurement, practical assessment increasingly demands the diagnosis of narrow, actionable attributes nested within broader proficiency domains.
For instance, one may aim at identifying whether a student masters finding common denominators or simplifying fractions within the broader domain of fraction subtraction ability (Tatsuoka, 1984).
text.formatted: For instance, one may aim at identifying whether a student masters finding common denominators or simplifying fractions within the broader domain of fraction subtraction ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Tatsuoka, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) were developed precisely for providing fine-grained, criterion-referenced profiles of attribute mastery rather than a single continuous ability estimate (e.g., de la Torre & Minchen, 2014).
text.formatted: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) were developed precisely for providing fine-grained, criterion-referenced profiles of attribute mastery rather than a single continuous ability estimate (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">de la Torre & Minchen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, most CDMs accommodate the influence of overall proficiency only indirectly.
In higher-order CDMs, a higher-order continuous ability influences attribute mastery, which in turn determines item responses (de la Torre & Douglas, 2004).
text.formatted: In higher-order CDMs, a higher-order continuous ability influences attribute mastery, which in turn determines item responses (de la <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Torre & Douglas, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In CDMs with a saturated attribute structure, dependence among attributes is instead represented directly through their joint latent-class distribution, without defining a higher-order ability (e.g., de la Torre, 2011; Henson et al., 2009; Junker & Sijtsma, 2001).
text.formatted: In CDMs with a saturated attribute structure, dependence among attributes is instead represented directly through their joint latent-class distribution, without defining a higher-order ability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">de la Torre, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Henson et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Junker & Sijtsma, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In neither formulation is a separate general proficiency dimension included directly in the item response function.
The main consequence of this modeling decision is that attribute mastery cannot be cleanly distinguished from general proficiency.
Because the model only specifies the influence of narrow attributes on item responses, any variance attributable to general proficiency is projected onto the attributes themselves.
The estimated mastery of an attribute therefore reflects a mixture of attribute-specific mastery and the proficiency level shared across the entire set of items.
The extreme case is strictly unidimensional data, in which attributes have no true influence on responses.

Fitting a CDM to such data will still yield diagnostic profiles, and these profiles may show substantial reliability even when little attribute-specific variation is present, because part of their apparent precision can be driven by true variance in the unmodeled general proficiency dimension (e.g., see Liu et al., 2018, for an application of CDMs to essentially unidimensional data).
text.formatted: Fitting a CDM to such data will still yield diagnostic profiles, and these profiles may show substantial reliability even when little attribute-specific variation is present, because part of their apparent precision can be driven by true variance in the unmodeled general proficiency dimension (e.g., see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Liu et al., 2018,</ref> for an application of CDMs to essentially unidimensional data).

text.text: This projection of general ability into attributes has theoretical and practical consequences.

At the theoretical level, a researcher may specify diagnostic categories on conceptual grounds that instead largely recover ordinal levels of a single underlying ability, rather than genuinely distinct competencies.

In this scenario, the estimated attributes may be highly intercorrelated (e.g., see Sessoms & Henson, 2018), with mastery profiles concentrated at the extremes (complete nonmastery or complete mastery), and little ability to distinguish which specific attributes are mastered among respondents sharing the same total number of mastered attributes.

text.text: In effect, the number of attributes mastered may become a function of the ordinal ranking of respondents on general ability.
At the practical level, this invites interpretation errors: a student may be directed to remediate a specific competency when the classification actually reflects overall proficiency.

Furthermore, the reliability of a mastery classification mixes attribute-specific information with shared variance from general proficiency, so an attribute may appear to be classified with high precision when that precision mostly reflects how well general ability alone predicts the response pattern.
Finally, at the statistical level, fitting an overparameterized model can reduce estimation efficiency, increase capitalization on chance, and limit classification accuracy (Ma et al., 2016).

text.text: These issues point to two unmet needs.
First, practitioners need attribute classifications whose meaning is not confounded with overall proficiency.
Second, researchers need a way to evaluate whether a hypothesized attribute structure carries diagnostic information beyond a single general dimension.

A way to reconcile general ability and discrete attribute mastery is a two-tier (bi-factor) structure, in which a continuous general proficiency dimension and a set of discrete attributes act as parallel, simultaneously operating tiers rather than a hierarchy of dependence.
In the bifactor CDM, the general dimension has a direct and independent effect on the item response probability.
This differs from the models above in that it requires no latent-class membership to define alternative response processes.
Instead, it provides a general measurement framework in which general ability and attribute-specific mastery are distinct and concurrent influences on item responses.

Because the bi-factor structure partitions the variance in item responses into generalability and attribute-specific components, a discrete diagnosis acquires a clearer meaning: mastery beyond what would be expected from general ability.
Consider two students with identical overall proportional reasoning proficiency (e.g., see Ma et al., 2020).

text.text: A bi-factor CDM can reveal that one has mastered constructing ratios and proportions beyond what general ability predicts, whereas the other's apparent mastery under a saturated or higher-order structure may be entirely accounted for by high general proficiency.

Such distinctions are directly relevant to instructional decisions (e.g., whether remediation should target a specific skill or reflects a broader ability deficit) in a way that standard CDMs, which confound the two sources of variance, cannot support.
Beyond scoring, the bi-factor structure serves as a diagnostic check on the attribute tier itself.

Under saturated or higher-order structures, attribute reliability can be high simply because attributes absorb variance from a general ability that is precisely estimated from the full item set, so such reliability is not evidence that the attributes are distinct.

Under a bi-factor CDM, general proficiency is modeled explicitly, and the reliability of the attribute-specific component reflects only how precisely mastery can be classified beyond what general ability explains.
High attribute-specific reliability therefore supports the separability of the diagnoses.
Low reliability indicates that the classifications carry little reliably recoverable information beyond general proficiency.

Because low reliability may also stem from few items per attribute or weak item discrimination for the attribute tier, it is best read as a signal to examine the attribute structure and test design, and high reliability as necessary, but not sufficient, evidence of separability.

This article introduces the bi-factor CDM (BF-CDM), a bi-factor extension of generalized CDMs in which a continuous general proficiency dimension is modeled alongside discrete attribute mastery profiles, with attributes reflecting specific competences shared by subsets of items as defined in the Q-matrix (Tatsuoka, 1983).

text.text: Like the SICM, the BF-CDM combines a continuous and a discrete tier in the item response function.
Unlike the SICM, which relies on a different (nominal responsebased) parameterization, the BF-CDM is a direct extension of the LCDM.

It is therefore closely tied to the family of LCDM-based CDMs and can benefit from the methodological developments built around them with little or no adaptation, whereas such developments would require adaptation for the SICM.
The BF-CDM targets the common CDM setting of dichotomously scored responses and skill-mastery attributes (de la Torre & Minchen, 2014; Sessoms & Henson, 2018).

text.text: In this setting, the BF-CDM makes it possible to evaluate skill mastery after partialling out general proficiency and provides a framework for evaluating the incremental diagnostic value of the attribute tier by assessing the reliability of the attributespecific component.
In this article, the feasibility of the BF-CDM is evaluated through a simulation study of parameter and item response function recovery.

Its practical relevance is then illustrated in a real-data application that compares the reliability of mastery and proficiency scores under unidimensional IRT, a saturated attribute structure CDM, and the BF-CDM, and discusses the implications for score interpretation and for evaluating the utility of the attribute tier.
It is first important to distinguish a saturated measurement model from a saturated attribute structure.

Saturated measurement models in CDMs allow a distinct response probability to be estimated for every latent group defined by an item, and often also allow the population latent class distribution to be estimated freely as a full multinomial (a saturated attribute structure, which in practice permits intercorrelation among attributes).
Examples of such models include the abovementioned LCDM (Henson et al., 2009), the generalized DINA model (de la Torre, 2011), and the general diagnostic model (GDM; von Davier, 2008).

text.text: Thus, the BF-CDM should be viewed as a general latent-variable framework within which a broad class of reduced CDMs can be embedded.
The latent variable structure of the BF-CDM implies a shift in how mastery status should be interpreted compared to saturated attribute structure or higher-order CDMs.

Under a classical CDM, mastery of attribute 𝑘 is an absolute classification, reflecting whether a respondent's response pattern provides sufficient evidence, against a fixed standard, that the attribute has been acquired.
Under the BF-CDM, by contrast, mastery status is more accurately interpreted as relative to a respondent's own general proficiency level.
That is, it reflects whether attribute-specific performance exceeds, equals, or falls short of what general proficiency predicts for the respondent.

As an example, under BF-CDM, for a respondent with low general proficiency, nonmastery of an attribute indicates weakness on that attribute beyond the low performance already implied by their general level.

Conversely, a respondent with low general proficiency classified as a master on some attribute exhibits a genuine relative strength, since overcoming a low general baseline requires sufficiently strong attribute-specific knowledge.
The same logic holds for high-proficiency respondents: a non-mastery classification for such a respondent reflects a specific deficit that persists despite a strong general baseline.

From a summative perspective, it may be reasonable to define mastery in absolute terms, against a fixed standard derived from the Q-matrix, even when that classification partly reflects general proficiency.
From a formative perspective, nonetheless, it may have great practical value to separate general proficiency from specific attribute mastery.
This distinction would allow feedback to address both the respondents' overall level of proficiency and their specific strengths and weaknesses relative to that level.
In other words, it could indicate whether the respondent would benefit from reviewing the test content in general, while directing efforts at particular attributes if necessary.
Additionally, the reliability of attribute classifications under the BF-CDM offers evidence on the validity of applying CDM framework to the data.
In essence, it indicates the extent to which variation in estimated attribute status reflects true variation in mastery rather than estimation error.

Under a saturated attribute structure CDM, high reliability of attribute classifications may reflect the true variation of a general proficiency dimension underlying attribute mastery, rather than variation specific to each attribute.

Under the BF-CDM, by separating the general and specific tiers, low reliability of attribute classifications, once the general proficiency component has been removed, would suggest that the remaining, attributespecific variation is largely random error rather than meaningful differentiation among examinees.

Beyond model fit statistics, accounting for attribute profile reliability provides evidence on the practical utility of the scoring framework, that is, on whether attribute-level scores contain information beyond what is already captured by the general proficiency estimate.

This simulation study aimed at evaluating the effect of relevant assessment characteristics on the recovery of BF-CDM parameters and item response functions.

Four factors were manipulated: sample size (𝑁 = 500, 1000, 2000), number of attributes (𝐾 = 3, 5), test length (𝐽 = 30, 60), and attribute-tier discrimination (manipulating guess and slip parameters) either low, i.e., 𝑃(𝛂 = 𝟎) and (1 -𝑃(𝛂 = 𝟏))~ 𝑈(.15, .25), or high, i.e., 𝑃(𝛂 = 𝟎) and (1 -𝑃(𝛂 = 𝟏)) ~ 𝑈(.05, .15).
This resulted in a fully crossed 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 design (24 conditions), each replicated 100 times, for a total of 2,400 simulated datasets.
The Q-matrices used for each condition contain items with different complexity (requiring varying numbers of attributes) and are properly identified.

Recovery was assessed for the general discrimination parameter, 𝛾 𝑗𝐺 , and for the 𝛌 𝑗 parameters of each item's latent groups.

For both parameters, three statistics were computed: (1) the correlation between estimated and generating values, (2) the mean absolute error (MAE), being the average unsigned difference between estimated and generating values, and (3) the mean error (ME), as the average signed difference between estimated and generating values.

Given the model's complexity, it is also important to assess how closely the entire estimated item response curves reproduce the true, data-generating curves, since parameter-level bias does not necessarily translate into distortion of modelimplied response probabilities.

This study illustrates the application of the BF-CDM to real assessment data.
The BF-CDM results are compared with those obtained from a unidimensional IRT 2PL model and a saturated LCDM in terms of model fit, reliability, and validity with external criteria.

In addition to the item responses, five items from the PISA 2000 student questionnaire were used as external criteria to evaluate the validity of the scores estimated under each model.
These variables capture students' reading habits, home reading resources, and self-reported performance in English.
Item 34 measures the amount of time students spend reading for enjoyment each day, ranging from no reading to more than two hours across five ordinal categories.

Item 35 assesses, through nine sub-items, attitudes toward reading using four-category agreement scales, covering aspects such as enjoyment of reading, reading as a hobby, willingness to discuss books, and difficulties sustaining reading.
The total score for Item 35 is calculated by summing the sub-item scores after reverse-coding negatively keyed items.
Item 36 measures how often students voluntarily read different types of material, including magazines, comic books, fiction, non-fiction, emails and web pages, and newspapers.
The six sub-items use five-category frequency scales ranging from never or hardly ever to several times a week.
The total score is calculated by summing the scores across the six sub-items.
Item 37 measures the number of books in the student's home across seven ordinal categories, from none to more than 500, providing an indicator of the home reading environment and access to books.

Finally, item 41 records students' self-reported marks in English from their most recent school report prior to the PISA assessment; these grades were discretized into six categories in the original PISA dataset.
The number of valid responses was 1,961 for item 34, 1,979 for item 35, 1,978 for item 36, 1,968 for item 37, and 845 for item 41.

text.text: The correlation between general proficiency scores estimated under the 2PL and under the BF-CDM was .99, indicating that the two models recover largely the same general dimension.
Point-biserial correlations between the LCDM attribute classifications and BF-CDM general proficiency scores were .70, .68, .72, .68, .74, and .68 for attributes 1 to 6, respectively.
Together, these results suggest that under a saturated attribute structure, LCDM attribute mastery classifications largely capture general proficiency rather than attribute-specific variance.

Consistent with this pattern of positive inter-attribute correlations, a large proportion of profile classifications under the LCDM concentrated in two classes: mastery of all attributes (𝜋 ̂𝑙 = .28) and non-mastery of all attributes (𝜋 ̂𝑙 = .17).

Together, these two extreme profiles accounted for 44% of respondents, consistent with attribute mastery behaving largely as a single all-or-none dimension rather than as six differentiated constructs.
Under the BF-CDM, by contrast, these two extreme profiles accounted for only 3% of classifications combined, with the remaining probability mass distributed evenly across the other profiles.

text.text: The BF-CDM was the best-fitting model by both deviance and AIC, indicating that the attribute-specific structure meaningfully improved fit over a unidimensional representation.
Under BIC, however, which imposes a stronger penalty for model complexity, the 2PL was preferred.
This mixed pattern admits two, non-exclusive readings.

Under one reading, general proficiency accounts for the majority of the variance in the data, with the additional attributespecific structure contributing comparatively little once model complexity is taken into account.
Under a second reading, the BIC penalty may be flagging an overfitting risk after the inclusion of the attribute tier.
Empirical reliability of the general proficiency factor under the 2PL and the BF-CDM was .86 and .84, respectively.
Under the LCDM, attribute-level reliability (expressed as 𝑅²) was .61, .53, .58, .62, .61, and .55, across the six attributes.

Under the BF-CDM, attribute-level reliability decreased substantively, taking values of .25, .19, .22, .32, .18, .32 across the six attributes, respectively.
This drop illustrates how most of what looked like attribute-specific reliability under the LCDM was in fact general-factor variance masked as attribute-specific information.

text.text: Finally, BF-CDMΔα indicates the incremental validity of the attribute tier, that is, the change in 𝑅² when predictions use all latent variables in the BF-CDM compared to the general proficiency alone.
This increment was at most 2.9%.

These results support the validity of the BF-CDM's score structure: by separating general proficiency into a continuous general factor and attribute-specific mastery profiles, the model gains predictive power over both a purely unidimensional representation and a purely discrete representation.
No statistically significant differences were found between the 2PL and LCDM on any of the criteria.

This article introduced the bi-factor cognitive diagnosis model (BF-CDM) as a framework for separating a continuous general proficiency dimension from a discrete, 𝐾dimensional attribute-mastery profile in the analysis of item response data.

Unlike saturated attribute structure or higher-order CDMs, in which the general dimension shapes item responses only indirectly, through its influence on the joint attribute distribution, the BF-CDM specifies both tiers as parallel, additive sources of item response variance.

This reformulation changes what a discrete mastery classification means: rather than an absolute statement about a fixed content domain, mastery under the BF-CDM is defined relative to what a respondent's general proficiency already predicts, and its reliability provides a direct check on whether the attribute tier contributes information beyond that shared, dominant dimension.

The simulation study demonstrated that item and person parameters, as well as the underlying response functions, can be recovered with good accuracy under the proposed marginal maximum likelihood procedure, across a broad range of realistic testing conditions.

As expected, recovery of the discrete-tier parameters and of attribute mastery classifications was most sensitive to sample size, test length, number of attributes, and attribute-tier discrimination, mirroring the results in the standard (non-bifactor) CDM literature.

Recovery of the general discrimination parameter, by contrast, was comparatively consistent across conditions, suggesting that estimation of the continuous tier is less demanding than estimation of the discrete tier, at least for the range of test lengths and attribute numbers considered here.
The real-data application illustrated one of the main contributions of the model in practical settings.
Under the saturated LCDM, attribute mastery classifications were strongly intercorrelated and dominated by two extreme, all-or-none profiles, and attribute-level reliability appeared moderate.

Once the shared general-proficiency variance was isolated under the BF-CDM, however, attribute-level reliability dropped substantially, indicating that most of what appeared to be attribute-specific precision under the LCDM was in fact general-factor variance recovered six separate times.

At the same time, BF-CDM scores showed a small but consistent validity advantage over both the 2PL and the LCDM against a broad set of external reading-related criteria, illustrating that separating the two tiers need not come at the cost of predictive power, even when the discrete tier itself carries limited independent information in a given application.

For test developers, these results suggest that attribute-level reporting in largely unidimensional data will require more indicators per attribute or more discriminating items than a blueprint designed for a single general ability.
By making this quantifiable, the BF-CDM offers test developers a means of judging whether a given blueprint can support attributelevel reporting.
Several limitations of the present work, and of this application, should be noted.
First, identification of the BF-CDM rests on the structural independence assumptions in Equations 4 and 5, which allocate all shared variance among all items to the general dimension by construction.

This is a strong assumption, directly analogous to the proportionality and local independence constraints underlying the bi-factor IRT model (Gibbons & Hedeker, 1992; Reise et al., 2010 Reise et al., , 2018)), and it is not statistically tested within the current framework.
text.formatted: This is a strong assumption, directly analogous to the proportionality and local independence constraints underlying the bi-factor IRT model <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gibbons & Hedeker, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Reise et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Reise et al., , 2018))</ref>, and it is not statistically tested within the current framework.

text.text: If some fraction of the association among attributes is not, in fact, mediated by general proficiency, the BF-CDM will still attribute it to 𝜃, and reported attribute reliabilities will be conservative accordingly.

Extensions incorporating partial correlations among attributes after accounting for 𝜃, or model comparisons against models that relax Equation 5, would help establish, in a given application, how much a drop in attribute reliability reflects this assumption rather than a genuinely low attribute-specific information.
Second, the real-data results should not be read as a general statement that discrete attributes are unnecessary once general proficiency is modeled.
Model-fit indices sent a mixed signal in the PISA application: AIC favored the BF-CDM over the unidimensional 2PL, whereas BIC favored the simpler model.

Because attribute-level reliability under a bi-factor structure is jointly a function of the true attribute-specific information in the data and of the adequacy of the Q-matrix used to define the attribute tier, the low reliabilities obtained here are consistent with either (a) the six PISA reading attributes carrying limited information beyond general reading proficiency, or (b) a Q-matrix that does not optimally isolate attribute-specific variance for this item set.

Sensitivity analyses using alternative, empirically or theoretically motivated Q-matrices (e.g., following the balancing procedures as in Nájera et al., 2020 Nájera et al., , 2021) ) would help disentangle these two explanations in future applications.

text.text: Third, the simulation study fixed the discriminative strength of the general dimension and varied only the attribute tier; how recovery depends on the relative discrimination of the two tiers, particularly when the general dimension is weak relative to the attributes, remains to be studied.

Relatedly, the current estimation procedure evaluates the model-implied likelihood over the full cross of quadrature nodes and attribute classes; while this grid remained computationally manageable for the number of attributes studied here, it will become prohibitive for tests measuring substantially more attributes, a limitation the BF-CDM shares with saturated CDMs more broadly.
Adaptive quadrature, Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro estimation, or variational approximations are natural candidates for extending the model to higher-dimensional attribute spaces.

Future work could extend the BF-CDM to polytomous responses, following the generalization of the LCDM to the GDM (von Davier, 2008), to multiple correlated general dimensions, or to longitudinal designs in which growth in general proficiency and in attribute mastery are of separate substantive interest.
text.formatted: Future work could extend the BF-CDM to polytomous responses, following the generalization of the LCDM to the GDM <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(von Davier, 2008)</ref>, to multiple correlated general dimensions, or to longitudinal designs in which growth in general proficiency and in attribute mastery are of separate substantive interest.

text.text: Because attribute-tier reliability under the BF-CDM offers a direct empirical check on the validity of a proposed attribute structure, it may also prove useful as a routine diagnostic tool during test development and Q-matrix validation, independent of whether a bi-factor structure is ultimately adopted for operational scoring.

In summary, the BF-CDM offers a way to answer a question that saturated and higherorder CDMs cannot directly address: how much of an attribute classification reflects genuine, attribute-specific mastery once general proficiency has been accounted for.

As illustrated here, the answer can be sobering, but it is precisely this capacity to distinguish real diagnostic value from an artifact of a dominant general factor that gives the model its practical relevance for both test developers and users of diagnostic score reports.
